title: No FOMO? Don't make this other classic stock-market investment mistake
text:
Published: Jan 26, 2018 11:55 a.m. ET Share 
How to handle your fear of the soaring Dow Jones Industrial Average 
By Analyst 
The media is full of reports of investors acting out of FOMO — “fear of missing out.” 
Many investors suffering from FOMO are making a classic mistake. I describe a better way in this article . The large response I received adds to the anecdotal evidence that many investors are making a second classic mistake, as they suffer from the fear of heights. This is the flip side of the fear of missing out. 
About a year ago, when The Arora Report laid out a scenario for Dow 30,000 , we got a fair bit of hate mail. Now we are getting some hate mail for staying bullish when the market is so high. Many investors are very concerned that the stock market has gone up in a straight line, valuations are stretched and technically the market is very overbought. Many in this group are making the second classic mistake — completely selling out of stocks. 
Before sharing with you a better way to deal with the fear of heights, let us first look at two charts to fully understand the issue and the better way. Two charts 
Please click here for the annotated chart of Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF DIA, +0.31% The chart shows the measured target for the Dow DJIA, +0.31% is 32,000. The first strong support is around Dow 18,000, or the level from which the stock market broke out after the 2016 election. This is about 8,000 points below where the Dow now trades. This indicates that although the bullish case for the market remains intact; there is also high risk from a technical perspective. 
In the interest of full transparency, this is the same chart that was published in my earlier piece about FOMO. 
Please click here for the annotated chart of S&P 500 ETF SPY, +0.50% during the 2008 stock market crash. Similar conclusions can be drawn from charts of the ETF QQQ, +0.76% that represents Nasdaq-100 NDX, +0.75% and the ETF IWM, -0.04% that represents the Russell 2000 RUT, -0.09% Please observe the following from the chart: 
•The crash didn’t happen all of a sudden. 
•There was a down trending channel before the steep drop. 
•There were lower highs before the steep drop. 
•There were lower lows before the steep drop. 
•The market reversed when the selling reached exhaustion levels and provided a great buying opportunity leading to a nine-year bull market. 
•The chart also shows signals given by The Arora Report to go to 100% in cash, buy inverse ETFs that go up when the market goes down and to go short for those who could before the crash. 
•The chart also shows the buy signals given by The Arora Report near the bottom. 
•To observe the down trending channel, lower highs and lower lows doesn’t require any special expertise, and an average investor can easily accomplish this. Contrast to 2008 
In contrast to 2008, the chart of the market now does not show a down trending channel, lower lows or lower highs. As a matter of fact, it shows the opposite: an up trending channel, higher highs and higher lows. 
Those who are interested in more sophistication in addition to rudimentary chart reading may consider paying attention to some or all of the 10 categories of inputs that we use at The Arora Report in our ZYX Global Allocation timing model. These 10 categories are listed here . 
To be fair, in 1987, the market crashed in one day. However, that was due to portfolio insurance and the lack of circuit breakers. In portfolio insurance, the falling market generated more selling. Circuit breakers stop trading when the market falls by a certain amount. Such a scenario is unlikely now. The second classic mistake 
The second classic mistake is selling everything and completely getting out of the market. We have seen investors sell out of everything thinking the market was too high when Dow was 12,000 and many gurus were predicting a crash. Since then we have seen this pattern every time the Dow gains another 1,000 points. The two-decision problem 
When investors get out of everything, they assume that they can get back at a lower price. This is harder than you think. You have to make two decisions right; first timing the exit and then timing the re-entry. The better way 
Investing doesn’t have to be an “all or none” decision. 
For those who are nervous, a better way is to scale out with small tranches if you are overexposed to the market. At this time it makes sense to hold on to most of the good positions. It is prudent to hold a fair amount of cash. The amount of cash held should very based on market conditions. You can add some sophistication by hedging. Further, investors ought to be looking at investing in sectors that are likely to do good in 2018 but are still relatively inexpensive. 
Investors ought to also review if they are overly concentrated in FAANG stocks. FAANG stocks are Facebook FB, +0.04% Amazon.com AMZN, +1.33% Apple AAPL, -0.10% Netflix NFLX, +0.65% and Google GOOG, -0.29% GOOGL, -0.43% and an overly concentrated portfolio would have 30% to 40% in these stocks.
